stories.headline: Kimi K3.1 Pro lands as a 3T-class open-weight model with a 1M-token context, weights due by Nov 4
stories.why_read: AI Top Story: an open-weight model now sits within a point of Claude Opus 5.5 on Terminal-Bench 4.0, which is exactly the open-source-LLM race you track.
body: Moonshot's Kimi team released K3.1 Pro, the first model in its K3.1 series, describing it as its most capable 3T-class open-weight model with a 1-million-token context window. A Highspeed variant runs 2 to 3 times faster. Both are live today on Kimi.ai, Kimi Work, Kimi Code, and the Kimi API, and the full weights are promised by November 4.

The headline number is coding: the blog reports 65.7% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, ahead of GPT-6 Astra at 58.2% and just behind Claude Opus 5.5 at 66.4%. The team credits much larger post-training compute and an RL stack rebuilt end to end, from long-context inference to sandbox infrastructure and rollout scheduling. It was the top AI story on Hacker News overnight with more than 900 points and over 550 comments.

stories.headline: NASA publishes a SpaceX milestone calendar for Artemis: prop transfer in Q1 2027, uncrewed lunar landing by Q4
stories.why_read: The Starship-to-the-Moon plan finally has dated checkpoints, and the first one, orbital propellant transfer, gates everything after it.
body: Per Sawyer Merritt's summary of a new NASA page, SpaceX's development milestones run quarter by quarter: a propellant-transfer demo and cabin operations testing in Q1 2027; a landing-leg demo, airlock demo, and barge to the Cape in Q2; the Artemis III mission plus uncrewed demo tanker flights and an uncrewed demo lander launch in Q3; and an uncrewed lunar landing in Q4, with more listed for 2028. NASA also shared a Starship lander concept of operations for Artemis IV.
The reply you reposted puts it plainly: prop transfer in Q1 is the one to watch, because everything after it depends on that demo working. If it slips, the whole ladder slips with it.

stories.headline: Calif shows a string of iPhone exploit demos at Hexacon: 'Today, we hacked what we'd set out to hack'
stories.why_read: One of the biggest HN threads of the day, and it lands in the same week as a pile of critical AI-assisted bug finds.
body: Security firm Calif posted a series of demos it revealed at the Hexacon conference in Paris, including attacks that move past third-party apps to iMessage, and says everything will be released in due time. The post is short on technical detail for now; the demos are the point.

The thread drew about 900 points and nearly 600 comments. Calif is also one of the teams working on AI-assisted vulnerability hunting through OpenAI's Patch the Planet program, which is why this one is getting read alongside this week's PHP and Brotli disclosures. Apple, for its part, is taking applications for its Security Research Device program through October 30.

stories.headline: Block's Dessa is a full-duplex speech model trained only on human conversation, no text at all
stories.why_read: You reposted Jack on this: a voice model that never turns speech into text, so it can hear tone, laugh mid-sentence, and talk over you like a person.
body: Block released a research preview of Dessa, which it calls the most authentic full-duplex speech model built so far. It was trained from scratch on human conversation audio alone, with no text and no pretrained models, and learned to hold a live conversation just by listening.

Block's argument is that today's voice assistants transcribe you and throw away everything text can't carry, like how you feel. Its demo clips show Dessa laughing the moment something is funny and getting louder when asked to speak up, behaviors nobody explicitly trained. There is a waitlist, and the HN thread is near 400 points.

stories.headline: Cursor agents can now drive your desktop, including the iOS Simulator, to test what they build
stories.why_read: A coding agent that can click through the app it just wrote closes the loop between writing code and checking it.
body: Cursor announced that its agents can now control your computer, driving desktop apps such as the iOS Simulator so they can exercise the features they build instead of stopping at a passing compile.

It fits the week's theme in what you've been reposting: the bottleneck is shifting from writing code to verifying it. An agent that can run the real app is one more way to close that gap without a human tapping through every screen.

stories.headline: Tesla registers 69 more Cybercabs in Texas, bringing the count to 420 in a 927-vehicle Robotaxi fleet
stories.why_read: Cybercabs are now more than 45% of Tesla's Texas Robotaxi fleet, a concrete sign the steering-wheel-free car is past the demo stage.
body: According to the X news summary, Tesla's latest Texas DMV filings add 69 Cybercabs, for 420 registered out of a Robotaxi fleet of 927 vehicles; the rest are 507 Model Ys. The fleet runs in Austin, Dallas, and Houston, with more cities planned.

On the Q3 call, Tesla said it aims to deliver the first Cybercabs to customers by December 2026, with customer-owned cars joining the network by mid-2027. Watching the registration count climb is the easiest way to check that ramp from Austin.

stories.headline: Dagger 1.0 enters beta after five years, as builders say CI can't keep up with agents
stories.why_read: Two posts you reposted back to back make the same case: if an agent has to push and wait for CI, the pipeline is the slowest part of the loop.
body: Solomon Hykes, Docker's co-founder, says Dagger is finally leaving v0 after five years, with 1.0 now in beta and a call for testers, noting a lot has changed for anyone who tried it before. Dagger's pitch is pipelines as code that run the same way locally as in CI.

Darren Shepherd framed why that matters now: CI needs to shift left, and if you have to push to execute CI you are wasting your agent's time, because traditional CI can't run at agent speed. For anyone running fleets of coding agents, local, reproducible pipelines stop being a nice-to-have.

stories.headline: Brotli decoder bug behind Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497, CVSS 9.2) also hits Python HTTP clients
stories.why_read: This one sits under almost every HTTP stack, and Python apps can pull it in without anyone noticing.
body: Aikido explains that CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write in Google's Brotli decoder, versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0, that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker corrupt memory and potentially run code with a crafted compressed stream. Node.js is affected through its bundled Brotli, which is the Node2Shell disclosure from earlier this week.

The post says OpenAI found it in February and that it works in both directions: a malicious client can take over an unpatched server, and a malicious server can take over an unpatched client. The fix landed in source back then but wasn't treated as a security issue until now. Because requests, httpx, and aiohttp load Brotli automatically when it's installed, the advice is to upgrade to Brotli 1.2.1 or the patched brotlicffi.

stories.headline: Oracle ships an emergency Java fix: a JSSE flaw lets forged TLS certificates pass as trusted
stories.why_read: Every JDK from 8 through 27 is listed, so this touches most Java you run.
body: Dan Vega flags CVE-2026-91403, rated CVSS 9.1: a flaw in JSSE, Java's TLS implementation, that lets a network attacker present forged certificates that get accepted as trusted. Java 8 through 27 are listed as affected, and Oracle shipped an out-of-band fix.
You reposted and bookmarked this one, and the advice is short: patch your JDKs now, including the ones baked into container images and build agents.

stories.headline: Is this the new cyber normal? A week of AI-found critical bugs, explained
stories.why_read: The best single read for making sense of the PHP, Brotli, and iPhone news, written by someone who says plainly he isn't a security expert.
body: Drew Silcock walks through the week's run of severe vulnerabilities, including two PHP remote-code-execution bugs found separately by Calif and Wiz, both using frontier models to find the bugs and build the exploits. One of them had surfaced in a 2024 PHP Foundation audit but was set aside because nobody could agree on a fix or show a working exploit; the post argues that turning a theoretical bug into a real exploit is exactly what LLMs are now good at.

Nick Dobos, in a post you reposted, put a number on the mood: by his count, 3% of all critical software bugs ever recorded were found in the last month. Silcock's essay is about what defenders should do when that becomes the normal week. For a live view, a new CVE tracker charts the daily count of published CVEs since 1999.

stories.headline: Google DeepMind researchers find 'Softmax Collapse' bugs in standard JAX and PyTorch implementations
stories.why_read: A floating-point flaw in one of the most-used functions in deep learning, with a small code fix.
body: Per the X news summary, Jon Barron and colleagues describe two failure modes they call Softmax Collapse and Softmax Cancellation, present in standard implementations across JAX, PyTorch, and textbooks, where floating-point limits distort gradients.

Their fixes are reported to remove loss spikes, speed convergence, and stabilize distillation without moving to higher precision. It's the kind of quiet numerical bug that shows up as mysterious training instability, so it's worth a look if you train anything.

stories.headline: WorldTUI: a 360M-parameter model that pretends to be a terminal, and mostly remembers what you did
stories.why_read: A fun, hands-on world-model experiment you can run in your browser, and a neat lesson in what small models can hold in their heads.
body: Simon Edwardsson fine-tuned a 360M-parameter language model to act as a terminal. There is no shell or filesystem behind it: each keypress goes in and the model predicts how the screen changes. It can create files, run vim and tmux, and play snake, and it usually remembers what you wrote a few commands later.

The biggest wins came from teaching it to repair its own mistakes and decoding screen rows in parallel. The demo is a 208 MB download that runs with WebGPU, and typing a typo like pythoon gives away that it isn't a real shell. Over 600 points on HN.

stories.headline: Astral wires uv and ty together: first-class Python script support and a single 'uv check'
stories.why_read: The fastest Python toolchain is turning into one integrated tool, which matters for both humans and coding agents.
body: Astral announced an experimental integration between uv, its package manager, and ty, its type checker and language server. Because uv understands your environment and dependencies and ty understands your code, together they give first-class support for standalone Python scripts on the command line and in the editor, plus a unified uv check command.
Astral frames it as the first step toward a toolchain where each tool still works alone but does more when combined. It's available in preview now.

stories.headline: Twelve years of distributed SQLite, from the person who started rqlite in 2014
stories.why_read: A first-hand history of a whole database category, and a clear explanation of why rqlite chose consistency over availability.
body: Philip O'Toole announced rqlite in September 2014: put a Raft log in front of SQLite and replicate every write across a cluster. As far as he can tell, it was the first open-source system to combine the two, and for years nobody else tried. Today distributed SQLite is a category with a dozen projects, some venture-funded and two acquired.

He writes down the version of the story that starts in 2014, including the move from goraft to HashiCorp's Raft in 2016 and the decision that never changed: rqlite is a CP system, so writes go through the leader and need a majority to acknowledge.

stories.headline: Marc Brooker: use LLMs to build animations that show how real systems fail
stories.why_read: One of the best systems writers shows metastable failures in real Postgres and etcd, and a Raft cluster losing writes over a lying fsync.
body: Marc Brooker describes a technique he's enjoying: having LLMs help build animations that make system behavior visible. One shows that a Raft cluster can lose writes if even one member's storage lies about fsync.

Others come from traces of real software. Postgres 16 in a microVM handles its load easily until a spike pushes the working set out of the page cache and it never recovers, and etcd falls into a storm of application resends after a write spike. His point is that production experience doesn't reliably shake these behaviors out, even in simple, non-distributed systems.

stories.headline: UUIDv7 timestamps aren't guaranteed to be time-ordered, or even close to the real time
stories.why_read: If you picked UUIDv7 to get creation-time ordering for free, read the RFC fine print this post quotes.
body: The post argues that the only property UUIDv7 strictly provides is uniqueness. RFC 9562 lets implementations alter the timestamp field and makes no promise about how close it is to the actual time, and the Postgres docs warn that an extracted timestamp may not match when the ID was generated.
So using the embedded time as your created-at column, or relying on IDs sorting in creation order, can bite you depending on which library made the ID. Lively HN thread with over 120 comments.

stories.headline: The 800 MHz story: from Nextel push-to-talk to SpaceX as a would-be fourth US carrier
stories.why_read: A great short history of one spectrum band that you reposted and bookmarked, with SpaceX at the end of it.
body: The Cybertruck Guy traces the 800 MHz band: Nextel owned it and used it for push-to-talk, Nextel merged into Sprint, Sprint merged into T-Mobile, and T-Mobile was supposed to sell it to Dish to rebuild a fourth US carrier.

In his telling, SpaceX bought it instead, which leads him to list the new big four as AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile, and SpaceX. That's his framing rather than an official one, but it shows how far Starlink's direct-to-phone ambitions now reach.

stories.headline: Tesla and SpaceX boards form independent committees to study a possible combination
stories.why_read: The biggest structural question hanging over both of Musk's companies now has a formal process.
body: Per the X news summary, both boards created special committees of independent directors to study closer ties, including a possible business combination that could value the combined company at $3.7 trillion. Musk supports the idea for synergies in AI, chips, robotics, and connectivity but is recused, and any deal needs committee, board, and shareholder approval.
Separately, SpaceX reported a $561 million unrealized gain on its Boring Company stake and $151 million of Megapack purchases from Tesla, a reminder of how intertwined the companies already are.

stories.headline: Tesla is building its own AI maps and navigation, rolling out with FSD v15
stories.why_read: Bad routing is one of the most common reasons drivers take over from FSD, and Tesla says it's replacing the whole stack.
body: On the Q3 call, Tesla VP of AI Ashok Elluswamy described a new AI-based mapping and navigation architecture built from fleet data with voice controls, dropping external map providers, according to the X news summary.
Features arrive with FSD v15 later this year or early next, starting with trip endpoints and growing to full routing, parking, and destinations.

stories.headline: Tesla raises financing rates early in Q4, which one investor reads as volume plus margin
stories.why_read: A small pricing signal you reposted, plus a pay-per-mile FSD idea that's worth a thought.
body: James Cat notes Tesla is raising financing rates, effectively a price increase, early in the quarter, and argues Q4 could be a double win of high volume and high margin.

In the same stream, Roland Pircher suggested Tesla charge for FSD per mile with a $99 monthly cap, on the theory that the drivers who use the car least are the ones who would benefit most from FSD but balk at a flat subscription.

stories.headline: Grok Imagine adds music generation for AI videos and images
stories.why_read: Grok's creative tools keep filling in the gaps, and soundtracks were a big one.
body: Per the X news summary, Grok Imagine now lets you generate full music tracks by describing genre, mood, instruments, and tempo, then trim and apply them to videos or images and save them for reuse.
It lands the same week Grok Imagine released the first seven-minute episode of its Odyssey series with Wonder Studios. Elon Musk agreed with praise for how fast the tool is improving.

stories.headline: Grok Bot users are building teams of specialized agents, and asking for dashboards and drag-to-context
stories.why_read: You're running exactly this kind of bot fleet, and several of the feature requests you reposted are in here.
body: The X news summary describes users building squads of persistent Grok Bot agents, each with its own cloud computer, browser, files, and terminal, for jobs from Japanese lessons to inbox cleanup to company workflows, with hundreds of thousands of weekly users.

Posts you reposted add the wish list: Mike P wants a shortcut to pull up a bot's dashboard directly, and praised the team for fixing mid-message voice dictation on iOS a day after he reported it. Alex mocked up dragging a bot out of the app onto a chart or an email so the context travels with it.

stories.headline: Kevin Weil's Warp Sciences raises $215M to build AI-run robotic chemistry labs
stories.why_read: AI for science moving from models to physical labs, with a former OpenAI exec and DJ Patil behind it.
body: Per the X news summary, Warp Sciences launched on October 22 with a $215 million Series A led by Lightspeed at an $865 million valuation. It builds AI-powered robotic labs in the US so biotech firms can test molecules faster, bringing chemistry work back from overseas with round-the-clock automation.
Co-founders include DJ Patil, Manohar Paluri, and Solomon Reisberg, and the pitch is that the labs also generate the data to train better models.

stories.headline: Physicists trap a single positron for months and measure its quantum states
stories.why_read: A clean physics result that could help answer why the universe is made of matter at all.
body: Scientific American reports that a team overseen by Gerald Gabrielse at Northwestern trapped one positron, the antimatter twin of the electron, for months at a time in a way that lets them study its quantum states. The positrons come from decaying sodium-22, and the hard part was slowing them down enough to capture.

The work appeared in Physical Review Letters. Precise comparisons between electrons and positrons are one of the ways physicists hunt for the asymmetry that left the world full of matter rather than antimatter.

stories.headline: Collagen-eating microbes may explain why the earliest soft animals fossilized and later ones vanished
stories.why_read: A neat evolutionary detective story about a gap in the fossil record.
body: Cambridge-led researchers looked at why Ediacaran fossils, from 579 to 539 million years ago, preserve soft-bodied animals in extraordinary detail when later soft creatures mostly disappear from the record.

Their proposed answer is the later evolution of microbes able to break down collagen, the structural protein in animal tissue. Before such microbes were common, soft bodies had a better chance of surviving long enough to fossilize.

stories.headline: Corgi is a tmux-style multiplexer that knows when your coding agents need you
stories.why_read: If you juggle several terminal agents, this is a practical tool for seeing which one is waiting on you.
body: Corgi keeps agents and processes running in the background like tmux, but marks each pane as working, needing you, or unread, with a key to catch up. It's built to work over SSH, supports image paste, and can be driven from any terminal.
It also ships a skill that teaches your agents how to use it.

stories.headline: Amdahl's Law explains why 10x faster coding gives teams only modest gains
stories.why_read: Useful math for any engineering leader being promised huge AI productivity numbers.
body: Arpit Bhayani's framing, per the X news summary: if coding is 30% of the work and AI makes it 10 times faster, the whole process speeds up only about 1.37 times, and faster code can clog review queues. Requirements, review, and debugging don't shrink on their own.
Optimists such as John Crickett counter that AI will raise demand for skilled engineers. It pairs well with the Dagger and CI posts above: speed up the rest of the pipeline or the gains stall.

stories.headline: Tim Bray on the little voice saying 'this would be a great job for Claude'
stories.why_read: A thoughtful, skeptical take from a veteran engineer that's worth reading even if you disagree.
body: Tim Bray, doing low-intensity work on his Quamina project, describes his running argument with himself about handing pieces to an AI. He's candid that he hasn't relied on it for substantial work, and that his biggest objections are ethical and economic rather than about capability.
He also guesses that once the bubble settles, many developers may end up on beefy desktops or cloud machines running open-weight models, which ties nicely to today's Kimi news.

stories.headline: Local Wikipedia shows only the articles about things within a half-hour walk of you
stories.why_read: A charming little tool and the day's most upvoted HN post; try it in Austin.
body: Ed Jefferson's site pulls geocoded Wikipedia pages near you. If there are fewer than 25 nearby, it takes the closest 25 within about six miles, and it caps at 500. Your location stays in the browser and isn't included in shared links.
It was the highest-scoring HN story in the batch, with about 1,400 points.

stories.headline: How is music possible? Henrik Karlsson on why tones in ratios can change how the world looks
stories.why_read: A gentle weekend read about math, feeling, and a car ride through a beech forest.
body: Henrik Karlsson starts with his nine-year-old closing her eyes during a Sámi joik on the radio, and asks why sounds arranged in mathematical relationships can make familiar trees feel otherworldly, the same way funny music makes a horror scene hilarious.
It's an essay rather than a news story, and it sits right in the physics-and-kindness corner of your pinned post.
